claims.statement: Default base-table capture uses AFTER statement triggers with transition tables and separate INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE events; legacy row mode is an alternative, and TRUNCATE has a separate statement trigger.
Trigger capture writes in the source transaction, so rollback removes captured changes and uncommitted images are not visible to other refresh backends.
Trigger builders stamp changes with pg_current_wal_insert_lsn rather than the potentially lagging write position, and statement builders use a statement-wide LSN.
Base and stream-table change buffers store flat typed row images and complete BYTEA identities; base buffers also carry changed-column metadata, and reserved source column names are escaped.
Ordinary captured updates are old-image D followed by new-image I, including primary-key changes and keyless updates; T and synthetic S records serve separate control purposes.
Change-buffer change_id sequences must remain CACHE 1 because same-row compaction ordering must not be inverted by per-backend sequence block allocation.
Base buffers are shared per source and use stable-name lookup with OID fallback, while stream-table buffers use changes_pgt_{pgt_id}.

The upstream refresh executor owns stream-table output capture after MERGE or explicit DML; graph capture uses the shared bound, and the merged output compatibility branch can recombine matching D/I pairs as U.

Foreign-table and materialized-view polling are opt-in capture mechanisms that compare saved snapshots with one materialized observation using EXCEPT ALL, serialize polls per source, emit local D/I deltas, and replace the snapshot from the same observation.
LSN ordering alone cannot prove MVCC visibility: a long-running source transaction can generate an early buffer LSN that must not be skipped by advancing a frontier while its rows remain invisible.

Scheduled safe-frontier probing samples a candidate LSN and backend xid/xmin plus prepared transactions; active writer fences inherit the previous candidate, persist while active, and bound monotonic safe progress, with no advancement past an unproven writer.

All coordinator holdback modes including none perform mandatory visibility probing; lsn byte mode adds a cap, and probe errors retain a valid previous bound or yield no bound rather than falling back to raw WAL progress.

Manual differential refresh reuses an immutable context bound or proves a READ COMMITTED candidate through source/descendant and buffer-schema writer-lock probing; active writers hold progress at 0/0, unsupported isolation fails closed, and frontier merge prevents backward replay.
FULL baseline protection locks managed source relations and partition descendants in OID order and additionally protects upstream stream storage and catalog boundaries.

Bounded source-position construction caps trigger positions at visible buffer progress and the safe bound, requires committed nonzero decoder positions for WAL, caps transitions at cutover, and rejects the legacy unbounded API.

Shared-source cleanup uses the minimum established consumer frontier, not the most recently refreshed consumer; consumers without baselines are excluded, absent or zero thresholds do not clean, and stream buffers have their own downstream minimum.

Base cleanup serializes minimum-frontier computation and cleanup with a per-source advisory lock, uses bounded heap deletion, and can detach consumed partitions; compaction must preserve shared consumer boundaries.

Change-buffer durability defaults to logged; unlogged buffers can be lost on crash and are not replicated, while sync uses logged tables plus registry-driven synchronous_commit on capture transactions; configuration changes do not automatically convert existing persistence.

Buffers have registry and synthetic sentinel metadata; invalid required capture state causes the scheduler to mark populated consumers for reinitialization and FULL refresh rather than silently continue differential maintenance.

WAL capture requests are reconciled per shared source through trigger, auto and wal modes; logical WAL and slot capacity are prerequisites, and transitions recheck regular-table, primary-key and REPLICA IDENTITY FULL eligibility.

The scheduler creates replication slots in pristine transactions and records publications and TRANSITIONING cutover state separately; trigger and WAL capture overlap until exact handoff proof, after which locked completion changes catalog mode before dropping triggers.

Current scheduler WAL capture uses test_decoding with pg_logical_slot_peek_changes and synchronously committed durable raw receipts, deduplicated by source_relid, lsn and data; unrelated messages are retained to verify the complete slot sequence.
Receipt replay applies source images to ordinary buffers and commits APPLIED status with those writes in a separate transaction from persistence and acknowledgement.

Acknowledgement consumes and verifies the exact recorded LSN/xid/data sequence only after APPLIED receipts exist, then records ACKNOWLEDGED and watermarks; confirmed slot progress allows finishing after a crash without consuming the slot again.

WAL fallback can follow timeout, eligibility loss, repeated poll failures or receipt failures; restoring triggers locks the source, attempts slot/publication removal, resets mode and cutover, and clears consumer frontiers while requiring reinitialization because triggers cannot recover undecoded history.

Receipt recovery tests terminate workers at persistence, replay, acknowledgement and post-slot-advance boundaries, restart the same database, require exact convergence against a journal, and check acknowledgement and repeated restart behavior.
